sentences: (PHOTO/XINHUA) MAGDEBURG — The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt with a record 44.4 percent of the vote, according to an exit poll released by public broadcaster ARD.

The AfD's 35-year-old state lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund hailed the result, declaring that "the people have sent a clear signal." Speaking to ARD, Siegmund also signaled a shift from his pre-election stance of only seeking office through an absolute majority, noting that his party is now open to a coalition.
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU), led by incumbent state leader Sven Schulze, suffered a heavy blow, plunging to 18.4 percent, down from 37.1 percent in 2021, the poll showed.

The newly formed Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) hovered right on the 5-percent threshold to enter the state parliament, while the business-friendly Free Democratic Party (FDP) crashed out with just 2.2 percent.

ALSO READ: Germany blames Russia for drone incursion, closes Russian Consulate General In Berlin, head of the Chancellery Nina Warken called the election outcome a "watershed moment" for the CDU, describing it on broadcaster ZDF as a "very, very difficult result." Warken also insisted that the federal government would resolutely press ahead with its planned reform agenda.
The Left party came in third with 9.3 percent, followed by the Greens with 8.7 percent and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) with 8.4 percent.
In the 83-seat state parliament, the AfD is projected to secure 39 seats, three seats shy of an absolute majority needed to govern alone.
It remains unclear how a viable state government will be formed.

tool.title: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406
tool.excerpt: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406. Recent observations are shedding light on the important role that active galactic nuclei (AGN) play in the production of high-energy neutrinos. In this study, we focus on one object, 5BZB J0630-2406, which is among the blazars recently proposed as associated with neutrino emission during the first 7-yr IceCube observations. Modelling the quasi-simultaneous, broad-band spectral energy distribution, we explore various scenarios from purely leptonic to lepto-hadronic models, testing the inclusion of external photon fields. This theoretical study provides a complementary testing ground for the proposed neutrino-blazar association. Despite being historically classified as a BL Lac, our study shows that 5BZB J0630-2406 belongs to the relatively rare sub-class of high-power flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). Our results indicate that interactions between protons and external radiation fields can produce a neutrino flux that is within the reach of the IceCube detector. Furthermore, the spectral shape of the X-ray emission suggests the imprint of hadronic processes related to very energetic protons.

That means that elections to the federal state parliaments are always significant in terms of national politics too.
In these elections, voters are of course deciding in the first instance on the composition of the parliament in their federal state and determining which parties will govern that federal state.

At the same time however, voters are indirectly determining who will have a seat and a say in the Bundesrat; the party that holds a majority in the federal state parliament forms the federal state government, and subsequently appoints from its ranks the Bundesrat members who will represent that federal state.

tool.title: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406
tool.excerpt: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406. Recent observations are shedding light on the important role that active galactic nuclei (AGN) play in the production of high-energy neutrinos. In this study, we focus on one object, 5BZB J0630-2406, which is among the blazars recently proposed as associated with neutrino emission during the first 7-yr IceCube observations. Modelling the quasi-simultaneous, broad-band spectral energy distribution, we explore various scenarios from purely leptonic to lepto-hadronic models, testing the inclusion of external photon fields. This theoretical study provides a complementary testing ground for the proposed neutrino-blazar association. Despite being historically classified as a BL Lac, our study shows that 5BZB J0630-2406 belongs to the relatively rare sub-class of high-power flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). Our results indicate that interactions between protons and external radiation fields can produce a neutrino flux that is within the reach of the IceCube detector. Furthermore, the spectral shape of the X-ray emission suggests the imprint of hadronic processes related to very energetic protons.

tool.title: AutoHVSR: a machine-learning-supported algorithm for the fully-automated processing of horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio measurements
tool.excerpt: AutoHVSR: a machine-learning-supported algorithm for the fully-automated processing of horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio measurements. This work proposes the AutoHVSR algorithm that allows for fully-automated processing of horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR) measurements, including those with zero, one, or multiple clear resonances. The AutoHVSR algorithm integrates robust signal processing and computational methods with state-of-the-art machine-learning models trained using a diverse dataset of 1109 HVSR measurements. The AutoHVSR algorithm demonstrates excellent performance by correctly determining the number of HVSR resonances for 1099 of the 1109 HVSR measurements (>99%) and predicting the mean resonant frequency of the correctly identified resonances with a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.05 Hz. Furthermore, the AutoHVSR algorithm was able to produce these predictions in 13 minutes (including HVSR processing time) compared to the 30 hours required for traditional processing (a speed up of 138). The AutoHVSR algorithm is further demonstrated on a challenging dataset from Canterbury, New Zealand that included many HVSR curves with multiple and/or ambiguous resonances. The AutoHVSR algorithm was capable of correctly determining the number of HVSR resonances for 113 of the 129 HVSR measurements (>87%) and predicting the mean resonant frequency of the correctly identified resonances with a RMSE of 0.10 Hz. The AutoHVSR algorithm produced these predictions under 2 minutes (including HVSR processing time) compared to the 4 hours required for traditional processing (a speed up of 120). Finally, while the AutoHVSR algorithm was developed using microtremor measurements where the horizontal components were combined using the geometric mean, it is shown to extend without modification to microtremor HVSR measurements where the two horizontal components are rotated azimuthally and to HVSR measurements from earthquake recordings. The AutoHVSR algorithm has been made publicly available in v0.3.0 of HVSRweb.

Authorities last year uncovered between 34,000 and 37,000 tons of waste, much of it imported from Italy in 2023 and 2024, at a site near the town of Gospic in Croatia’s Lika region.

tool.title: “Ready for the Homeland” in Croatian media: Commemorations, victory, and foundation
tool.excerpt: “Ready for the Homeland” in Croatian media: Commemorations, victory, and foundation. This article analyses the media discourse surrounding the WWII fascist salute Za dom spremni (ZDS) in the aftermath of two national commemorations that took place in Croatia in spring 2020: Jasenovac and Operation Flash (Bljesak). In spring 2020 Zoran Milanović, the newly elected President of Croatia, adamantly criticized the presence of the salute, associated with the collaborationist Ustaša regime, at the two commemorations, calling for its removal and ban. This led to heated reactions from war veterans and politicians who considered Milanović’s actions unacceptable and offensive towards the memory and legacy of the 1990s war, which triggered a wider debate regarding Croatia’s post-war national identity. The object of the analysis is the discourse surrounding the salute as it emerges in opinion pieces published in weekly and daily newspapers in April, May, and June 2020. With the salute becoming an increasingly prominent part of negotiating national identity and tailoring political agendas, investigating how it is justified, disapproved or otherwise challenged in the media is an aspect that deserves more attention. Relying on insights from discourse studies, the article sheds light on various statements that (de)legitimize the salute and consequently particular actors and actions associated with it. With the help of semiotics of culture wider signification tendencies and dominant discourse(s) upon which the national selfdescription has been built are identified. The article contributes to scholarship on hate speech and contested symbols in the post-Yugoslav space and their (mis)uses in societies struggling with traumatic legacies.

tool.title: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406
tool.excerpt: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406. Recent observations are shedding light on the important role that active galactic nuclei (AGN) play in the production of high-energy neutrinos. In this study, we focus on one object, 5BZB J0630-2406, which is among the blazars recently proposed as associated with neutrino emission during the first 7-yr IceCube observations. Modelling the quasi-simultaneous, broad-band spectral energy distribution, we explore various scenarios from purely leptonic to lepto-hadronic models, testing the inclusion of external photon fields. This theoretical study provides a complementary testing ground for the proposed neutrino-blazar association. Despite being historically classified as a BL Lac, our study shows that 5BZB J0630-2406 belongs to the relatively rare sub-class of high-power flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). Our results indicate that interactions between protons and external radiation fields can produce a neutrino flux that is within the reach of the IceCube detector. Furthermore, the spectral shape of the X-ray emission suggests the imprint of hadronic processes related to very energetic protons.

tool.title: “Ready for the Homeland” in Croatian media: Commemorations, victory, and foundation
tool.excerpt: “Ready for the Homeland” in Croatian media: Commemorations, victory, and foundation. This article analyses the media discourse surrounding the WWII fascist salute Za dom spremni (ZDS) in the aftermath of two national commemorations that took place in Croatia in spring 2020: Jasenovac and Operation Flash (Bljesak). In spring 2020 Zoran Milanović, the newly elected President of Croatia, adamantly criticized the presence of the salute, associated with the collaborationist Ustaša regime, at the two commemorations, calling for its removal and ban. This led to heated reactions from war veterans and politicians who considered Milanović’s actions unacceptable and offensive towards the memory and legacy of the 1990s war, which triggered a wider debate regarding Croatia’s post-war national identity. The object of the analysis is the discourse surrounding the salute as it emerges in opinion pieces published in weekly and daily newspapers in April, May, and June 2020. With the salute becoming an increasingly prominent part of negotiating national identity and tailoring political agendas, investigating how it is justified, disapproved or otherwise challenged in the media is an aspect that deserves more attention. Relying on insights from discourse studies, the article sheds light on various statements that (de)legitimize the salute and consequently particular actors and actions associated with it. With the help of semiotics of culture wider signification tendencies and dominant discourse(s) upon which the national selfdescription has been built are identified. The article contributes to scholarship on hate speech and contested symbols in the post-Yugoslav space and their (mis)uses in societies struggling with traumatic legacies.

tool.title: Long-Term Care Workforce in Croatia: A Qualitative Study on the Potential Role of Immigration
tool.excerpt: Long-Term Care Workforce in Croatia: A Qualitative Study on the Potential Role of Immigration. The deficit of workers, especially skilled nurses, is a growing concern in the long-term care (LTC) sector. In developed economies, the share of migrant workers in LTC has been steadily increasing. The goal of this paper is to explore the potential role of immigration in tackling the LTC workforce shortage in Croatia, a country marked by a “care drain”, through semi-structured interviews (N=13) with stakeholders from the government, the City of Zagreb, non-governmental organizations, professional associations, nursing homes and the academic community. There is a high consensus among interviewees that immigration is one of the possible solutions to the LTC labour shortage in Croatia. However, in order to keep the native workers and attract foreign ones, working conditions should be improved and wages raised. It is also crucial to develop integration policies and provide foreign workers with good professional training and quality language education. Key words long-term care; care workers; nurses; migration; population ageing; Croatia

sentences: Current Population Overview Size, Density, and Distribution from 2021 Census The 2021 Census of Population, Households and Dwellings recorded Croatia's permanent resident population at 3,871,833 as of August 31, 2021, encompassing the 20 counties and the City of Zagreb.

[17] 20th-Century Changes Including Wars and Socialism The population of Croatia, encompassing the territories of Croatia-Slavonia and Dalmatia, stood at approximately 2.66 million in the 1910 census conducted under Austria-Hungary .

[18] World War I inflicted severe demographic tolls, with Croatian troops mobilized into the Austro-Hungarian forces suffering estimated military casualties of around 137,000 deaths alongside civilian losses from disease, famine, and the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic, contributing to a net population decline evident in the 1921 census at roughly 2.56 million.

[20] Overall war-related losses for Croatia's population hovered around 10-15% when accounting for direct combat, genocide , and post-war purges, though the 1948 census recorded 3.78 million, reflecting baby boom births amid territorial adjustments and suppressed mortality reporting under emerging communist rule.

[72] This rapid exodus reduced the Serb proportion of Croatia's population from 12.2% in 1991 (about 580,000 individuals in a total of 4.7 million) to 3.2% by 2021, representing a direct loss of roughly 4–5% of the national population and entrenching long-term underpopulation in affected rural enclaves.

[89] Ethnic and Cultural Composition Dominant Ethnic Groups and Proportions According to the 2021 census conducted by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, Croats constitute 91.63% of the total population, equating to 3,547,614 individuals out of 3,871,833 enumerated inhabitants.

[95] Census Year Serb Population Percentage of Total 1991 581,663 12.2% 2001 201,631 4.5% 2011 186,170 4.4% 2021 123,892 3.2% Linguistic Diversity and Regional Variations Croatian dominates as the mother tongue of 95.25% of the population according to the 2021 census conducted by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics.

[104] Religious Landscape Predominant Faiths and Secularization Trends The 2021 Croatian census recorded Roman Catholicism as the predominant faith, with 78.97% of the population identifying as Catholic, a decline from 86.28% in the 2011 census .

[12] The first systematic Habsburg census in 1857 recorded approximately 2.1 million inhabitants across Croatia-Slavonia, with density averaging 37 persons per square kilometer, underscoring a predominantly rural, agrarian society where over 80% lived in villages tied to subsistence farming and limited commerce.

[28] The tide turned with Croatian military operations Flash (May 1995) and Storm (August 1995), which reclaimed lost territories but prompted a rapid exodus of approximately 250,000 Serbs from Krajina and Slavonia , reducing the Serb share of Croatia's population from 12.2% in the 1991 census to 4.5% by 2001.

[68] Although return migration was high—around 66% of Croatian emigrants to America repatriated—the net outflow still contributed to village depopulation and strained local economies, with Croatia's population hovering near 2.5 million around 1900.

[92] [93] Census self-identification patterns show some fluidity, with ethnic re-identification contributing to the reinforced Croat majority alongside factors like differential migration and fertility rates; for instance, the Serb population declined by over one-third from 2011 to 2021, partly attributable to such shifts.

[91] Minority Groups, Historical Shifts, and War-Related Changes The Serb population underwent the most significant historical shift among Croatia's minorities during the 1991–1995 war, dropping from 581,663 (12.2% of the total population) in the March 1991 census to 201,631 (4.5%) by the 2001 census.

[116] Post-1995, Croatia's overwhelming Croat majority (over 90% by 2021 census) has underpinned low levels of interfaith conflict, with constitutional guarantees of religious equality and separation of church and state enabling minority practice amid secular trends.

[5] Historical Demographics Pre-Modern and 19th-Century Population The territory comprising modern Croatia experienced significant demographic fluctuations during the pre-modern era, marked by Ottoman-Habsburg conflicts from the 15th to 17th centuries that caused widespread depopulation through warfare, forced migrations, and epidemics.

[10] [11] By the late 18th century, demographer Jakov Gelo's reconstructions place the population at over 1 million, reflecting modest natural increase amid high fertility (typically 5-6 children per woman) offset by mortality from events like the 1738-1739 plague and periodic subsistence crises.

[19] Interwar growth was modest, reaching about 2.66 million by the 1931 census, buoyed by returning migrants and natural increase, though ethnic tensions simmered amid Serb-Croat political frictions in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia .

[19] [22] Census data reflect steady growth: 3.94 million (1953), 4.16 million (1961), 4.43 million (1971), and 4.60 million (1981), but at decelerating rates from 1.5% annually post-1953 to under 1% by the 1970s , attributable to these systemic shifts rather than exogenous shocks.

[30] [31] Post-war refugee dynamics included partial Croat returns, with over 200,000 displaced Croats repatriating by 1996, though net population fell from 4.78 million in 1991 to 4.44 million in 2001, reflecting unrecovered losses from deaths, non-returning emigrants, and suppressed vital rates.

[36] The national population density averaged 68 inhabitants per square kilometer across Croatia's land area of 56,594 km², with marked regional variations: higher concentrations in urban centers and coastal zones, contrasted by sparse inland rural districts.

Urban settlements, defined by DZS as cities and larger towns, accommodated about 58% of the populace (roughly 2.24 million), underscoring a shift toward agglomeration amid widespread rural exodus, with the remaining 42% in smaller municipalities and villages.
[35] Recent Annual Estimates and Short-Term Trends As of mid-2024, the population of Croatia was estimated at 3,866,233 inhabitants, comprising 1,882,564 males and 1,983,669 females.

Death Rates, Life Expectancy, and Mortality Patterns Life expectancy at birth in Croatia reached 78.5 years in 2023, reflecting a gradual increase from prior decades despite an aging population structure.

[59] [55] Suicide mortality, while showing a long-term decline since 2004, rose to 15.7 per 100,000 population in 2021 , with higher incidence among males and in rural regions linked to economic distress and limited mental health access.

Age Structure, Dependency Ratios, and Population Pyramid Croatia's population age structure in 2023 reflects an advanced stage of demographic aging, with an inverted pyramid shape characterized by a narrow base representing low fertility and a widened apex indicating prolonged life expectancy.

Between 1890 and the outbreak of World War I , an estimated 500,000 individuals emigrated from Croatian territories, with the United States as the principal destination; this wave substantially reduced rural populations, as emigrants were predominantly young males from agricultural backgrounds.

[74] Contemporary Emigration, Brain Drain, and Economic Drivers Following Croatia's accession to the European Union on July 1, 2013, the country experienced accelerated emigration , particularly among working-age individuals, resulting in an estimated net population loss of approximately 250,000 people through migration by 2023.
[84] Despite this inflow, emigration of Croatian citizens continued at significant levels, comprising 64.8% of total outflows and exacerbating labor shortages amid an aging population.

[91] By 2011, Serbs numbered 186,170 (4.4%), further falling to 123,892 (3.2%) in the 2021 census, reflecting self-reported data that challenges narratives inflating pre-war shares or framing reductions exclusively as forced displacement without evidence of strategic evacuation and natural demographic attrition.

[97] In addition to native languages, surveys on language knowledge indicate that approximately 0.7% of the population speaks Russian, placing Croatia 19th in Europe for the proportion of Russian speakers, according to 2024 European Commission data.

[99] Minority languages have experienced decline since the 1990s, driven by post-war emigration, intergenerational shifts toward Croatian, and urbanization, reducing speakers of Italian from over 10,000 in 1991 to around 3,000 by 2021 in official tallies.

[102] National minorities with sufficient population thresholds (e.g., eight pupils per grade) access bilingual or native-language classes, yet such programs cover only a fraction of students, prioritizing Croatian proficiency for integration.

[112] The demographic impact was profound: pre-war Croatia (within 1931 Yugoslav borders) had Serbs comprising about 24% of the population, many Orthodox; Ustaše actions, estimated to have killed 300,000 to 350,000 Serbs across NDH territories through genocide , contributed to a sharp reduction in the Orthodox share post-war, fostering greater Catholic dominance amid reprisals and migrations.

[114] Serb forces' sieges of Catholic-majority cities like Vukovar in 1991 involved targeted killings and expulsions of Croats, invoking Orthodox solidarity; Croatian counteroffensives, culminating in Operation Storm in August 1995, expelled over 200,000 Krajina Serbs in a rapid ethnic cleansing operation, reducing the Serb population from 12% in 1991 to under 5% by 2001.

[106] [117] Socioeconomic and Health Indicators Education Attainment and Literacy Rates Croatia maintains a high adult literacy rate of 99.3% as of 2021, with males at 99.7% and females at 99.0%, reflecting near-universal basic literacy achieved through compulsory primary education .

[59] [133] Urbanization, Housing, and Family Structures Approximately 59% of Croatia's population lived in urban areas as of 2024, reflecting a steady urbanization trend driven by internal migration and economic opportunities in larger settlements.

Lifelong singlehood remains relatively uncommon in Croatia, with the majority of adults eventually forming long-term partnerships; rates of permanent singlehood hover around 5%, consistent with EU averages and reinforced by cultural and religious factors promoting marriage and family formation.

Economic and Policy Implications of Aging and Depopulation The escalating old-age dependency ratio in Croatia , projected at 56.2% by 2050 and 62.2% by 2070, intensifies fiscal pressures by increasing the burden on a shrinking working-age population to support retirees through taxes and contributions.

tool.title: Long-Term Care Workforce in Croatia: A Qualitative Study on the Potential Role of Immigration
tool.excerpt: Long-Term Care Workforce in Croatia: A Qualitative Study on the Potential Role of Immigration. The deficit of workers, especially skilled nurses, is a growing concern in the long-term care (LTC) sector. In developed economies, the share of migrant workers in LTC has been steadily increasing. The goal of this paper is to explore the potential role of immigration in tackling the LTC workforce shortage in Croatia, a country marked by a “care drain”, through semi-structured interviews (N=13) with stakeholders from the government, the City of Zagreb, non-governmental organizations, professional associations, nursing homes and the academic community. There is a high consensus among interviewees that immigration is one of the possible solutions to the LTC labour shortage in Croatia. However, in order to keep the native workers and attract foreign ones, working conditions should be improved and wages raised. It is also crucial to develop integration policies and provide foreign workers with good professional training and quality language education. Key words long-term care; care workers; nurses; migration; population ageing; Croatia

tool.title: AutoHVSR: a machine-learning-supported algorithm for the fully-automated processing of horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio measurements
tool.excerpt: AutoHVSR: a machine-learning-supported algorithm for the fully-automated processing of horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio measurements. This work proposes the AutoHVSR algorithm that allows for fully-automated processing of horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratio (HVSR) measurements, including those with zero, one, or multiple clear resonances. The AutoHVSR algorithm integrates robust signal processing and computational methods with state-of-the-art machine-learning models trained using a diverse dataset of 1109 HVSR measurements. The AutoHVSR algorithm demonstrates excellent performance by correctly determining the number of HVSR resonances for 1099 of the 1109 HVSR measurements (>99%) and predicting the mean resonant frequency of the correctly identified resonances with a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.05 Hz. Furthermore, the AutoHVSR algorithm was able to produce these predictions in 13 minutes (including HVSR processing time) compared to the 30 hours required for traditional processing (a speed up of 138). The AutoHVSR algorithm is further demonstrated on a challenging dataset from Canterbury, New Zealand that included many HVSR curves with multiple and/or ambiguous resonances. The AutoHVSR algorithm was capable of correctly determining the number of HVSR resonances for 113 of the 129 HVSR measurements (>87%) and predicting the mean resonant frequency of the correctly identified resonances with a RMSE of 0.10 Hz. The AutoHVSR algorithm produced these predictions under 2 minutes (including HVSR processing time) compared to the 4 hours required for traditional processing (a speed up of 120). Finally, while the AutoHVSR algorithm was developed using microtremor measurements where the horizontal components were combined using the geometric mean, it is shown to extend without modification to microtremor HVSR measurements where the two horizontal components are rotated azimuthally and to HVSR measurements from earthquake recordings. The AutoHVSR algorithm has been made publicly available in v0.3.0 of HVSRweb.

tool.title: Long-Term Care Workforce in Croatia: A Qualitative Study on the Potential Role of Immigration
tool.excerpt: Long-Term Care Workforce in Croatia: A Qualitative Study on the Potential Role of Immigration. The deficit of workers, especially skilled nurses, is a growing concern in the long-term care (LTC) sector. In developed economies, the share of migrant workers in LTC has been steadily increasing. The goal of this paper is to explore the potential role of immigration in tackling the LTC workforce shortage in Croatia, a country marked by a “care drain”, through semi-structured interviews (N=13) with stakeholders from the government, the City of Zagreb, non-governmental organizations, professional associations, nursing homes and the academic community. There is a high consensus among interviewees that immigration is one of the possible solutions to the LTC labour shortage in Croatia. However, in order to keep the native workers and attract foreign ones, working conditions should be improved and wages raised. It is also crucial to develop integration policies and provide foreign workers with good professional training and quality language education. Key words long-term care; care workers; nurses; migration; population ageing; Croatia

tool.title: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406
tool.excerpt: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406. Recent observations are shedding light on the important role that active galactic nuclei (AGN) play in the production of high-energy neutrinos. In this study, we focus on one object, 5BZB J0630-2406, which is among the blazars recently proposed as associated with neutrino emission during the first 7-yr IceCube observations. Modelling the quasi-simultaneous, broad-band spectral energy distribution, we explore various scenarios from purely leptonic to lepto-hadronic models, testing the inclusion of external photon fields. This theoretical study provides a complementary testing ground for the proposed neutrino-blazar association. Despite being historically classified as a BL Lac, our study shows that 5BZB J0630-2406 belongs to the relatively rare sub-class of high-power flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). Our results indicate that interactions between protons and external radiation fields can produce a neutrino flux that is within the reach of the IceCube detector. Furthermore, the spectral shape of the X-ray emission suggests the imprint of hadronic processes related to very energetic protons.

sentences: El resto de territorios, denominados zona C (que incluyen las colonias judías de Gaza y Cisjordania, la zona del Valle del Jordán y las conexiones terrestres entre las ciudades palestinas y que suponían al principio el 72-74% de Cisjordania), debían estar según estos acuerdos bajo responsabilidad exclusiva del Estado de Israel.
[ 14 ] [ 15 ] [ 16 ] [ 17 ] El término «Territorios Palestinos Ocupados» incide en la ocupación militar y la administración israelí de Cisjordania , la Franja de Gaza y Jerusalén Este desde 1967.

[ 18 ] [ 19 ] En 2024, la Corte Internacional de Justicia declaró que el control ejercido por Israel en los territorios palestinos ocupados ―Cisjordania, Gaza y Jerusalén Este― viola las leyes internacionales, instando al gobierno israelí a cesar la actividad colonizadora, así como a reparar el daño causado por la ocupación.
Por último, sectores extremistas árabes llaman Palestina también al territorio del actual Estado de Israel, además de la Franja de Gaza y Cisjordania.

Dichos sectores creen que los territorios de Judea y Samaria y, en menor medida, Gaza son parte integral del Estado de Israel por razones históricas, morales y religiosas, y deberían ser anexados por el mismo.

[ 40 ] La guerra provocó miles de desplazados en ambos sentidos: entre 600.000 y 800.000 árabes de la zona israelí fueron obligados a desplazarse a las vecinas Gaza y Cisjordania, y también a otros países árabes más alejados, dando origen al problema de los refugiados palestinos , que todavía hoy perdura.

La ocupación israelí de Gaza y Cisjordania es, de hecho, el principal foco de tensión que desde sus inicios motivó numerosos atentados de fedayines contra civiles israelíes, tanto dentro como fuera de Israel (secuestros de aviones y ataques como la masacre de Múnich ).
↑ «Gaza se asfixia: Los efectos del bloqueo israelí en los palestinos» .

Territorios Palestinos es una de las denominaciones que recibe el territorio formado por las regiones de Cisjordania (5655 km² de superficie terrestre [ 1 ] y 220 km² del mar Muerto ) y la Franja de Gaza (365 km²).

[ 1 ] Este término es particularmente usado en mayor medida en Israel y en cierta medida en Estados Unidos , mientras que en otros países en general se suelen usar los términos de Estado de Palestina o sencillamente Palestina .

En 1994, conforme a los acuerdos de Oslo entre la Organización para la Liberación de Palestina (OLP) y el Gobierno de Israel , se creó la Autoridad Nacional Palestina , la cual fue designada para controlar tanto la seguridad como la administración civil en las áreas urbanas de los territorios y la administración civil en las áreas rurales.
En 2005 Israel se retiró de la Franja de Gaza y, como consecuencia, la administración de dicho territorio pasó de facto a Hamás .

Esta denominación puede referirse a los territorios gobernados por la Autoridad Nacional Palestina (ANP), [ cita requerida ] pero también puede incluir todo el territorio de la Franja de Gaza , Cisjordania y Jerusalén Este .

[ 2 ] [ 3 ] La denominación no incluye los Altos del Golán (ocupados hoy por Israel, pero que pertenecen a Siria), ni las Granjas de Shebaa (reclamadas por Líbano y Siria ), ni la península del Sinaí , conquistada por Israel en 1967 y devuelta a Egipto en 1979 tras el Tratado de paz egipcio-israelí .

[ 7 ] [ 8 ] [ 9 ] [ 10 ] Terminología [ editar ] Territorios Palestinos Ocupados [ editar ] Artículo principal: Territorios ocupados por Israel El grueso de los Estados miembros de la ONU considera que estos territorios están bajo un régimen de ocupación militar.

[ 11 ] Según el criterio de Naciones Unidas , este término designa una única entidad política, compuesta por dos territorios físicamente separados ( Franja de Gaza y Cisjordania ) y de los que Israel deberá retirarse bajo un tratado de paz que garantice también su seguridad y el «derecho a vivir en paz bajo unas fronteras seguras».
Para la CIJ , la creación de la Autoridad Nacional Palestina no ha modificado la situación de ocupación por parte de Israel.

En 2005, Israel desmanteló unilateralmente sus asentamientos en la Franja de Gaza , en una decisión sin precedentes llamada Plan de retirada unilateral israelí o «Plan de desconexión», por lo que el término no reflejaría toda la realidad de los territorios.

Además, Israel sigue controlando el movimiento de mercancías y personas en las fronteras y dentro de los territorios, manteniendo un bloqueo que está considerado por Amnistía Internacional como un castigo colectivo a toda la población de la Franja de Gaza.

[ 20 ] En septiembre de 2024, La Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas adoptó una resolución no vinculante redactada por la delegación palestina que exige a Israel que ponga fin a «su presencia ilegal en el territorio palestino ocupado» en un plazo de 12 meses.
El embajador palestino calificó la votación como un punto de inflexión «en nuestra lucha por la libertad y la justicia», mientras que su homólogo israelí la calificó como «terrorismo diplomático».

La confusión se debe a que en el transcurso de esta guerra Israel no solo conquistó los Territorios Palestinos, sino que también conquistó la península del Sinaí , Jerusalén Oriental y los Altos del Golán , los cuales incorporaría a la administración israelí en 1981, siendo una extensión territorial reivindicada por Siria , excepto las granjas de Shebaa que son reivindicadas por el Líbano .

Desde finales del siglo XX , numerosos países y organismos internacionales designan a los territorios palestinos como « Palestina », en referencia al Estado independiente reivindicado por la OLP en la Franja de Gaza, Cisjordania y Jerusalén Este.
El territorio a administrar incluía todo lo que es actualmente Israel , Cisjordania con Jerusalén Este , la Franja de Gaza y Jordania .
Afectó a aproximadamente el 53% de la población árabe de Palestina y al 82% de los árabes que residían en la parte de Palestina que se convirtió en Israel.

Para la CIJ , la creación de la Autoridad Nacional Palestina no ha modificado la situación de ocupación por parte de Israel.

En 2005, Israel desmanteló unilateralmente sus asentamientos en la Franja de Gaza , en una decisión sin precedentes llamada Plan de retirada unilateral israelí o «Plan de desconexión», por lo que el término no reflejaría toda la realidad de los territorios.

Además, Israel sigue controlando el movimiento de mercancías y personas en las fronteras y dentro de los territorios, manteniendo un bloqueo que está considerado por Amnistía Internacional como un castigo colectivo a toda la población de la Franja de Gaza.

El embajador palestino calificó la votación como un punto de inflexión «en nuestra lucha por la libertad y la justicia», mientras que su homólogo israelí la calificó como «terrorismo diplomático».

La confusión se debe a que en el transcurso de esta guerra Israel no solo conquistó los Territorios Palestinos, sino que también conquistó la península del Sinaí , Jerusalén Oriental y los Altos del Golán , los cuales incorporaría a la administración israelí en 1981, siendo una extensión territorial reivindicada por Siria , excepto las granjas de Shebaa que son reivindicadas por el Líbano .
